paragraphs: Building on its recently announced plans to bring original Xbox games to PC , Microsoft is also planning to let developers bring their Xbox 360 games to PC as well, according to a leaked document, seen by The Verge , that was sent to developers recently. Xbox 360 games will be able to run on the next-gen Project Helix console, “Xbox PCs,” and handheld devices, the document says.

Microsoft has already said that Helix will play PC games , so making these older Xbox titles available on PC helps build a broader Xbox library that can travel between devices, similar to what’s already possible with Steam. Creating all these digital licenses also helps set up for a future of consoles without disc drives; Sony has already declared game discs dead , and Microsoft may follow .

With 360 games, developers can opt into making them backward compatible, and they will have control over things like a game’s price and if it’s available on Game Pass. The feature is expected to have a “gradual” rollout between 2027 and 2028 “across next-gen devices.” The “full launch” of original Xbox games on PC is also set for October 2026; the initial program announced in July included just four games.

The document also includes details about a way for players to get a digital version of a game that they already own on a physical disc, which The Verge ’s Tom Warren reported on in July . The document says that if a player puts an Xbox One or Series game on disc into an Xbox One or Series X console with a disc drive, they’ll be granted a digital license that’s bound to “that disc and the player’s account.” The license will stay with a player across Xbox devices, but if the disc “changes hands,” the license will transfer to the new person. That should mean that gamers can still trade and sell discs; once the original owner of a disc does so, they can’t play the digital version they got from that disc anymore.

According to the document, a public beta for the disc-to-digital program was set for July with general availability set for August. We understand Microsoft had originally planned to test its disc-to-digital program with Xbox Insiders in July, but the beta was delayed. It’s unclear if the timeline of August general availability is still accurate.
The planned changes follow Microsoft’s major Xbox “reset” announced in July , which included thousands of layoffs and the company selling off four studios.

draft_context.description: Microsoft Edge has a lot of built-in features that go unnoticed. Read Aloud has been part of Edge for a long time, and I use it all the time to review articles and listen to content. But after weeks of testing, I understand how Edge's Read Aloud feature stacks up against a dedicated tool for text-to-speech. Speechify launched a Windows app earlier this year that adds real-time text-to-speech and voice typing to PCs. There was already a Speechify web extension, which is what I used for testing here. Speechify shared Premium access with me to help me assess their app and extension, so I've had several months to get used to them and compare them to alternatives. Interestingly, Speechify and Read Aloud in Edge excelled in different areas. Accuracy and cadence Speechify (left) offers smoother natural voices and page navigation, but Edge's built-in Read Aloud toolbar (right) handles basic text-to-speech for free. (Image credit: Future) Read Aloud supports a large library of voices. These are fun to play around with since there are quite a few English options sporting different accents. All of the voices marked as "Natural" in Read Aloud sound fluid and are easy to understand. Occasionally, the feature will pause for a moment as it decides where to jump to next on a page (more on that below). Read Aloud finds text well and presents pages using voice, allowing you to multitask or absorb content through both reading and listening. While Edge's voices sound fluid, Speechify's voices sound more natural. They sound as if a voice actor is in a booth reading to you. There's a bit more bass in each voice and more depth than what's in Edge. Speechify has several celebrity voices, which to be honest I'm not too fussed about. I don't need robot Gwyneth Paltrow to read me the latest Xbox news, but it's an option if you'd like her to. Voices in Speechify are labeled based on their key characteristic, such as "Velvety" or "Easygoing." The "Resonant" Dominic voice would be a great choice to read the next Sarah J. Maas novel, but I don't think he's the best option for tech news. Because Speechify's voices are clear and natural-sounding, you can play them at faster speeds before they sound ridiculous. I'm able to play Speechify voices at over 2.2x speed and still understand them. Edge's Read Aloud voices max out at around 2x speed before they're difficult to understand. Dealing with the modern web The modern web is full of inserts, page breaks, ads, and other components. When you read an article online, you rarely see a large block of uninterrupted text. In fact, my editor would tell me off if I published a piece of just text. In order for articles to be visually engaging, publishers place block quotes, embedded posts, videos, and other items. When you read an article, you scan over certain content without thinking. If you spend a lot of time on the web, you've learned what should be read as part of an article, such as a block quote, and what is separate, like a list of related pieces. Microsoft Edge's Read Aloud feature has not learned the same lessons. It will jarringly jump between the main text of a piece and a "You May Like" section. In contrast, Speechify sticks with the main text of an article and hops over inserts that are off-topic. In my testing, Speechify correctly identifies the content I'd like read, such as block quotes, but bypasses things I'd want to circle back to later and click. Both Read Aloud in Edge and Speechify hopped past ads in my experience, which is nice. This app adds voice typing and text-to-speech to Windows. It can read PDFs, web pages, or documents and can be used to convert spoken words to text with correct punctuation. A subscription also gets you more features within the web extension . Note that the free version of the Speechify app is limited to slower listening speeds, fewer voices, and text-to-speech (voice typing requires Premium). Voice typing is free within the extension. View Deal Is Edge Read Aloud better than Speechify? Speechify works well and sounds natural, but it's difficult to justify its cost when Edge can do much of the same for free. (Image credit: Speechify | Edited with Gemini) Edge's Read Aloud feature is surprisingly solid for a free tool that's built into Microsoft's browser. If you only care about listening to the web, it's the better choice for most people. Speechify is not worth its subscription cost if you only plan to use it to listen to articles out loud. A large portion of Speechify's value comes from its dictation features. Don't get me wrong, Speechify is very good at reading websites and documents out loud. I prefer how it handles ads, text blocks inserted into pieces, and other website components. I also prefer the voices in Speechify. But Edge's built-in Read Aloud feature works well and is free. Paying $29 per month is a large investment to listen to articles. If you need to dictate text and listen to articles, I'd suggest trying Speechify. Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more. ]]>

draft_context.source_title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO. This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder , because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all. Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable. But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop. That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads. This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you’re gonna like it. Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of Bluesky. Welcome to Decoder. Thank you. Thanks for having me. I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there’s something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. I know that you are a believer in it in the same way that you believed in the web when you were the CEO of Automattic, which is the company that makes WordPress. So let’s just start at the very start. Describe what you think Bluesky is today and what you think the opportunities with these new kinds of networks are. Bluesky today is really two things. There’s the Bluesky app, which is what a lot of people are familiar with. It’s a social network. We think it’s a better social network. It’s more human focused, doesn’t have ads. It doesn’t have algorithms. But more importantly, underneath Bluesky is an open protocol called AT Protocol. And Bluesky is only one of now over a thousand apps built on that protocol. The whole point of Bluesky was to demonstrate that this open protocol could scale and attract other builders, building lots of apps, lots of social experiences that all interoperate and connect with each other, which is what we believe the future of social media should look like. It’s what is actually going to make social media something that we believe in, which is that the future of social media should serve the public good. That is what motivates us, and that’s why we built the protocol first and then the app. There’s a lot in there already that is just pure Decoder bait, including the notion that Bluesky, the product, and the ATmosphere and AT Protocol, the standard, are all intermixed in one company that you now run. Right next to that is maybe the purest Decoder bait of all: the fact that Jay Graber, who was the CEO of Bluesky – she was on the show about two years ago – stepped down into the role of chief innovation officer. You were the interim CEO, and now after four months, you are the full-time CEO. Fundamentally, that is just the story that Decoder loves to tell the most. Talk me through that. What made you step in as the interim CEO, and why did you decide to become the full-time CEO? It’s actually really cool and inspiring that a founder, after she worked on this for six years, got it off the ground. She started inside Twitter, got it out of there, made it an independent thing. There are a lot of reasons why Bluesky is facing long odds and she got into this place, and then felt like it’s at a scale now where [it’s in] her sweet spot, the things that she loves working on, which is vision, innovation, new ideas. She felt pulled back towards building, especially also because of the advent of AI and how AI and AT Proto can interoperate. She felt like that’s what she wants to go work on, and it’s time to find somebody else for the CEO job. I was already involved with this project because I met the team a little bit over two years ago, probably around the same time Jay was on your podcast. We became investors through True Ventures. So I’ve been following it as an investor, supporting it. The team approached me and said that my background with WordPress and open source was a really good fit. And so I agreed to be interim CEO initially because I was still a general partner at True and it’s a firm I helped build. It’s an amazing firm that I didn’t want to leave behind. But also, at True, we’ve had this model where we’ve moved back and forth between operator and investor. I did that while I was running Automattic. So I stepped into it. After working on it hands-on for a few months, it just got more and more fun, more and more energizing. You just feel the momentum. Also, True just switched to a new fund. So actually the timing was good where I could say, “Okay, I will switch my true role to part-time, become a venture partner,” which is what I used to be when I ran Automattic, “and I’ll go all in at Bluesky.” Tell me about the difference between being the interim CEO and the full-time CEO. When you’re the interim CEO, it feels like there are probably some boundaries in what you can do. And then the full-time CEO can obviously do everything that a full-time CEO can do. What did you feel like the boundaries were as interim CEO? On the inside, it hasn’t felt very different. I actually think the move to drop the “interim” is more important on the outside, especially for the ATmosphere and the AT Proto community, and people building on this platform and in this ecosystem just to say, “No, I’m here for the duration. This isn’t just some interim gig and then somebody else is going to show up.” So I felt like, to the outside, that makes a big difference. On the inside, the job really hasn’t changed much.. So many of my conversations here in Decoder are really about the timescale of decisions. I’ll make the comparison to my newsroom because it’s easy and it’s easy to understand. Our reporters make decisions in like 30-minute increments. A story comes up, they write it, they publish it, they move on to the next thing. I make decisions maybe in like week- or month-long increments. What are we going to cover? Where are the resources going to go? It seems like in the interim CEO role, the timescale of those decisions is necessarily short or it has the appearance of being short. And then I’m reading your note that you published when you became the full-time CEO. In the very beginning of it, you say we’re at the very beginning of the story with a decade of exciting work ahead. And I’m wondering if the timescale of the decisions you’re making now are a decade. Yeah. It touches on something really fascinating with this project. In general with decision making, one of the frameworks I really like is the reversible and irreversible decisions. A lot of decisions we make are actually reversible. I like to optimize to just make those decisions quickly and then make sure you can undo the decisions if you need to change them. And then there are a few decisions that really do have very long-term implications. They’re much harder to reverse. With this project in particular, there are decisions made at this protocol level that we’re going to have to live with for a long time. There’s a part of the company in this community that thinks very, very, very long term. This is a protocol that is going to be around for decades already. It’s in enough use that it’s going to be around for a long time. Those decisions you really need to be careful about. Then it goes all the way to things we try in the product that work or don’t work. I wasn’t in the interim mindset as much because I am also an investor in the company, so I care very much about the long-term picture. What attracts me to this whole endeavor is that it can have a really important long-term impact. I always think about, okay, how will this play out? Does this truly serve the core mission? It’s okay to make some of these harder decisions now that won’t pay off for a long time because this is going to take a while. It’s not just one company. It’s already thousands of others that are building together. That’s just a different timeframe and decision-making process than your typical just “go fast, scale as quickly as possible” [methodology]. I like it. I’m comfortable with it. I just want to stick with Bluesky, the company that is both responsible for the standard and the protocol, and the product that a lot of end users love and sometimes hate. That is the core tension of the company. The user base of Bluesky is or is not interested in the development of AT Protocol, is or is not interested in the wider ATmosphere. Under Jay’s tenure, the company was very focused on building out the protocol because the product literally could not exist unless the protocol was robust enough to stand up the product. You could see that back and forth. I have always felt that the company is far more interested in the protocol than the product, that the product was merely there to show what people could do. But now the product is big. It might be waxing or waning. It will come to whether you need to turn it into TikTok or not. Tell me where you, as a CEO with a decade-long vision for all of this, see the balance inside of Bluesky between the product, the thing that looks like a Twitter app, and the protocol, the thing that should enable thousands upon thousands of other social experiences? I see the Bluesky app and the product as enabling the ATmosphere. It’s an on-ramp, or maybe a lobby to the ATmosphere where it’s just a great way to get lots of people in, get people exposed to the idea, and then realize as you use the product, “Oh, there are other things here. This isn’t just a microblogging app.” An example from the last couple of months that’s gone super well is this format called Standard Site that emerged. The history of that is that Bluesky’s a microblogging app. People are asking for longer-form posting. A bunch of other apps started popping up that were for newsletters and blogging. In particular, three apps called Leaflet , Pckt , and Offprint . They got together and said, “Hey, why don’t we define a format for all of us to work together on the ATmosphere for all of the posts that we publish?” We looked at it and said, “Great, we can now take that and surface it in our app.” So now, if you’re posting a blog post on Leaflet, it just shows up in the Bluesky app and we can make that a seamless experience. This went over really well to the point where now WordPress is supporting Standard Site and lots of other publishing platforms. They’re realizing the benefit of, “If I just publish to this new format now, it’s going to show up and work across all these other platforms without me having to do anything.” It’s caused this really nice ripple effect throughout the ecosystem where people can work together just by using this format. Nobody has to do deals with each other. Nobody has to get permissions and no money has to change hands. And it’s just taken off. I’m hoping more and more Bluesky users will see those kinds of integrations and go, “Oh, cool. I’m not just getting Bluesky content here. I’m getting content from all these other apps, all these other networks. And it just works. I don’t have to do anything. I don’t have to go sign up for 10 different apps. It’s just one signup, one account, and it just works.” You’re describing two different kinds of things. There’s a lot of work to be done at the protocol level. There’s a lot of work to be done to support new kinds of experiences like Standard Site. Then there’s Bluesky, a product which has 45 million people, and probably needs to be substantially bigger if it wants to be the aggregator for a massive network that can displace some of the other social products out there. That needs to be a lot of things to a lot of people. It needs to find different kinds of product market fit. How big is Bluesky the company now, and how is it structured to point in two different directions? We’re now at 50 people, still very small. The biggest challenge is clearly trying to do everything you’ve described with a small team. We do have an ecosystem of hundreds and thousands of others working on it, so that helps. We do our best to coordinate everyone. I would say we’re making good progress. We’re seeing good momentum, especially on the ATmosphere side. The things we look at are the number of daily active apps on the network, which has doubled since the beginning of the year. It’s about to hit a thousand. We look at SDK downloads for our tools that have tripled. It’s going to hit a million downloads a month by later this year. Those are the numbers that show that not only is it scaling, but we’re able to scale it with the team that we have. How is that team structured? About 50 people, all remote, structured into small teams. I’m a big believer that six to eight person teams, highly aligned, highly incentivized, and motivated are the way to get things done. Probably the only way to get things done. There are three core product teams. There’s the app team that deals with the Bluesky app. There’s the ATmosphere team that does all the developer-facing stuff. And then there’s a third product team called the exploration team, and that’s a new team that Jay has stood up and is running. We actually just launched a new version of the product they’re working on, Attie. Think of it as AI layered on top of the ATmosphere and what you can do with that. Those are our three core product teams, and they’re each customer-facing. Consumer-facing, developer-facing, and then we’ll find out from the AI product what the market fit is there. We have a bunch of support teams that support those three core teams and that are pretty typical. We’ve got a legal team, et cetera, et cetera. I would say it’s a team that’s a very low ego, high agency. That is kind of the ethos. Low drama, just a lot of get-shit-done energy. Really collaborative. Whenever I think about new social products and how they might scale, especially with explosive user growth – up until recently, the conventional wisdom is you’ve got to scale trust and safety and moderation linearly with the size of your user base. Maybe we’re going to add AI to this and that linear relationship will break, or maybe it’ll actually get even more costly because token spend will get more costly than having human moderators, or there’ll be more false positives and we’re going to be even angrier. So you have to have more humans in the loop. It’s really unclear to me how that’s going to work. You’ve obviously been scaling Bluesky as a consumer social product. Then you have the complexity of, “We’re hooking onto lots and lots of other products that are putting content in front of people.” How does the moderation layer work? And have you seen it be a linear increase in cost with the size of the network and the user base? Moderation is huge in any social product. In addition to our 50-person team, we do have contractors that help us with moderation. What we’ve done differently is that our whole moderation system is composable or pluggable. It’s not just us that can label content and moderate it. Anybody can do it and add labels. It’s part of the protocol. Anybody else who builds products can decide if they want to use those labels or not. So if somebody on our moderation team labels something as, let’s say, AI slop, everybody else who’s building in this ecosystem can take advantage of that piece of data. They don’t have to, but they can. So what we’re seeing and what we’ve seen is we have our moderation team, but then there are other teams that have decided to moderate label content the way they want. For example, maybe the first non-Bluesky project on the protocol was Blacksky. And it’s now become a thriving company on its own. It’s a team building all kinds of interesting things. And they started out by saying, “Hey, we want to build a version of this network that is optimized for Black users and their needs. And we want to have our own moderation policies.” And they are able to do that and plug that in. But everything they’re doing is still part of the larger network. And now there are hundreds and thousands of these kinds of systems. This has really helped where the moderation burden isn’t all on one team that has to scale and look at everything. There should be lots of different teams and lots of different systems because each network, each community has its own idea of what moderation should look like. So we feel like this kind of distributed moderation approach is more powerful. That said, yes, we’re continuing to scale up ours, but it’s manageable. It’s a lot of work, but it’s manageable. It’s worth it when the whole network can benefit from it. The next part of that story that’s going to be really interesting is that the biggest thing we’re actually working on with AT Proto, the next evolution of the protocol, is private data. We all know that the public square, public social networking has reached a certain scale. And there are a lot of people who want to retreat into more private spaces. We’ve seen explosive growth in group chats. We’re all in a million group chats. This has been the number-one request from our community, from our developers: “Let us build more private, membership-based, various versions of private spaces on this protocol.” We’re in the middle of building that. It’s a community effort. It’s rolling out very soon. Now, moderation moves and gets broken up into even more and smaller spaces. People can decide, “If I don’t like a network or I don’t like the way it’s moderated, [I can] go start my own.” Go start your own community. That’s the most interesting thing ahead of us, because right now everything on AT Proto is public. It can only be used for a completely public product. Once we enable private data, I think that it’s like 10 or 100X the number of use cases we can serve. Not to be reductive, but I think it’s useful to talk about this in comparison to other social products people might be more familiar with. With AT Protocol right now and the ATmosphere, everything is very public. The models in my head are Twitter, and RSS, and massive broad-based publishing platforms, right? One-to-many. I think what you’re describing is much more like a Reddit style approach, where you have smaller, closed communities. Some of them can be totally private unless you’re invited in. And yet, they’re still on the ATmosphere in some way. Is that right? That’s right. The trade-off has traditionally been that if you want to be on a launch network, you have to be on a public network. Or if you want to control, have ownership over your own community, you have to set up your own thing. You have to run your own server or you have to run your own forum. You don’t have to, you can just run it by yourself, or you can plug into the federation, into the Fediverse. That’s how their system works. It works really well. They have a lot of successful governments who want to set up their own server infrastructure and run their own community infrastructure. AT Proto has a different goal. We don’t have a server at the heart of it. We have the PDS, the personal data server that is your data. The heart of AT Proto is personal identity and portability and ownership of that so that whatever you create and the social graph that you create is owned by you and lifts wherever you want to host it. It’s really a federation of millions and millions of these tiny little personal servers that can all talk to each other. That works if your social product is focused on people, not on an entire server with a community on it. So a slightly different shape. They interoperate too. There’s something called Bridgy Fed that connects these two worlds together. So if you’ve built products on this yourself, if you want to post or publish across all of it, you can and the end user doesn’t even have to know. That’s the beauty of an open protocol: you shouldn’t have to. Consumers of this should never even hear about these new protocols. Because it’s one of these things where you have to get the protocol right and it has to be open, but then people should just forget about it. It should just disappear. The examples we use a lot are email and websites. If I’m on Outlook and you’re on Gmail, we can just email each other. You never think about the fact that those are two completely separate systems. It just works. But on social media, it just doesn’t work that way. If you’re on Instagram and I’m on TikTok, we can’t talk to each other. You have to do everything five different times and on five different apps, and it’s crazy making. If we get this right at the protocol level, that just goes away. All this stuff just works just like email does or just like websites do. Our job is to make all of that work under the hood, but nobody has to think about it. In the end, you just have one account, you log in anywhere and it just works, and all your friends are there and all your data’s there. And you never have to be locked in again into somebody’s system [where] you can’t leave. This is very nice, but it’s rare that two standards that nominally seek to achieve the same thing coexist forever. There are not two Bluetooths, there are not two Wi-Fis. There are not even two webs. People can argue with me about how many webs there are, but there are not even two webs. Do you expect ActivityPub and AT Protocol to coexist? Do you expect, I don’t know, Bluesky to be able to show content from Mastodon servers and then slowly eat ActivityPub as a protocol? That’s one very common pattern that happens in these situations. Or do you expect long-term coexistence? I expect long-term coexistence because both of these protocols have enough users and use cases that want to continue on. They can talk to each other when you want, but that’s not the main use of it. There are a lot of people who run ActivityPub instances who don’t even want to talk to other Mastodon servers. They just want to run their own thing. They don’t want to talk to AT Proto, but they can if they want. I don’t know what a good example is from other platforms. But they’re both going to be around for a long time and they’re just slightly different tools. They’re both in the social space, but they’re different tools that you reach to for different types of use cases. I’ll put it this way: In my mind, both can be wildly successful, and it’s not one or the other. AT Proto doesn’t need to eat ActivityPub to be successful, or vice versa. We’ve already seen that. I want to end by talking about the consumer app a little bit more. We’ve talked a lot about the protocol, the ATmosphere, the standards. We’ve gotten all the way to the internet engineering task force in this conversation. We’ve been in the weeds of how the technology works and how it’s governed. And right next to that is, well, it’s an election year here in the United States. And a lot of people truly believe that Bluesky is the wild progressive social media network and it is a bubble of one kind. X is a very different kind of bubble. It’s the hard-right network that has vastly more AI-generated anime porn on it. There’s not some thing that is actually the global town square. That thing has maybe gone away and all the social networks have fragmented. Do you want Bluesky to have the reputation it has? Do you want it to get bigger? Do you think that the right answer is someone starts a MAGA Bluesky and it interoperates the way that it needs to? This is the perception of the consumer product. Do you want that to change, and how would you change it? Yes, we definitely want that to change. It is already changing. It certainly wasn’t designed to attract one specific group of people. It works for anyone. What we see is there is a lot of political discourse on Bluesky and any of these open networks. People are very engaged. What we’ve seen in the lead up to the election so far – we’ve hosted a lot of live election feeds, and we see a lot of really good feedback from our users, a lot of engagement, a lot of, “This is actually really interesting content about this topic.” Whereas on other platforms, I think these election topics just get completely overwhelmed by slop and spam. It’s just noise and chaos. What we’re focusing on is to deliver a live experience. We do it around elections. We do it around sports as well, very successfully, where the people on the network that participate get a really good experience and get really good content. Once we have that, then hopefully we can just keep expanding to more and more types of users and use cases. We’re an open network for anyone and we don’t want to serve just one type of user base. I’ve seen it already in the last few months, really trend in the right direction where we just have more and more people show up and build their own corners of the network. It sort of balances out over time. We don’t just have a few topics you’re super deep on, but it just gets more and more diverse. In my opinion, yes, it’s a public square, but we don’t need everybody talking at the same time. Policy is very loaded, but if you’re super into sports, you’re not going to be into all sports. I’m super into the San Francisco Giants, so that’s what I want to follow. I don’t need to follow all of sports, and that’s fine. It can be like that with all topics. It just needs to be civil and positive and we need to have the tools that if it goes off the rails, people can regulate it and can have a good experience instead of it just devolving into a shouting match. By “people can regulate it,” you mean people can moderate their own feeds, not regulators can moderate speech? 100%, yes. Just checking. That’s important. Build their own feeds, pick their own feeds. We have very good tools for people to mute and block. We spend a lot of energy on making sure it stays positive because again, we’re interested in social media that actually serves the common or the public good. That’s not going to work if it’s just people yelling. You’ve talked a lot about the network. Even in this answer, I said Bluesky the app has this reputation, and you started talking about the network. It’s true, the network can serve everybody. Anybody can start whatever kind of app on the ATmosphere they want and they can go target the users they want. But I want to push you again on Bluesky the app. The thing that has a brand that exists out in the world that is totally divorced from the technical specifications of the ATmosphere. There is Bluesky the app and it does have a reputation. Do you want more users from X to leave X and join Bluesky and expand what that brand is for people? Yes. It can stay on X too. You don’t have to pick one or the other, but yes. Have you talked to Elon about federating X? I suspect he’s not interested. No, same answer with Threads. It would be full circle, right? Bluesky started inside Twitter, and then Twitter went away and became X. And then if X adopted AT Proto, then the whole original idea of the project would actually come to fruition. Yeah. This is Jack Dorsey saying Twitter wants to be AT Protocol, not a product. Here we are, and that’s Bluesky in big ways, but it is also a product. People know what that logo means. Political pundits say “the Bluesky crowd,” and that signifies whatever they want it to signify. I’m just wondering if you want to break that branding in any meaningful way. Yeah, we want to expand it. “Breaking” is maybe the wrong word, but yes, we want to expand more and more so that Bluesky means not just one thing, not just liberal politics, for example. I will point to sports as an example from the last year. We’ve made a very concerted effort to bring on sports leagues and sports writers, and it’s worked really well. There are a ton of sports conversations now on the app, and those people come here for the sports, not for the liberal politics. It’s possible to expand. In politics, it’s probably our hardest challenge because we have one type of user base there that’s very active. That’s good too. They are super active, and they’re very much at the forefront of politics and very engaged and very informed. But we can just keep adding more communities so that it balances out. It feels like we’re going to have to have you back, particularly as these private communities launch, to talk about where things go from here. But this has been great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thank you very much for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO.

This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder , because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all.

Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable.

But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team.

Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop.

draft_context.source_title: Post-quantum authentication to origins is now supported
draft_context.description: Cloudflare's Authenticated Origin Pulls and Custom Origin Trust Store now support post-quantum authentication. Here we’ll explain how you can configure fully post-quantum secure mutually authenticated TLS connections to your origin server, dive into the engineering details of how we built it, make a shameful confession, and finally explain how this work fits into our overall post-quantum migration roadmap. Reaching a major milestone Our focus for the past several years has been in deploying post-quantum encryption to protect against harvest-now/decrypt-later attacks, where an attacker quietly stockpiles your encrypted data with the hope of decrypting it in the future with a quantum computer. However, recent breakthroughs in quantum computing and cryptanalysis pulled the timelines for upgrading to post-quantum cryptography forward across industry and government and have caused us to shift our attention to deploying post-quantum authentication , to protect against attackers who will soon be able to use quantum computers to break classical credentials and carry out impersonation attacks. In a previous post, we announced that Cloudflare is targeting 2029 for full post-quantum security, and laid out several milestones to hit along the way. We have reached the first of those milestones: our Authenticated Origin Pulls and Custom Origin Trust Store products now support post-quantum (PQ) authentication via Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) signatures to protect connections between Cloudflare and customer origin servers. The origin connection is different When a client visits a website proxied by Cloudflare, there are typically two connections involved. The first connection is from the visitor (e.g., a browser) to Cloudflare. If the request can be served from Cloudflare’s cache or triggers any blocking rules, Cloudflare might respond directly. Otherwise, Cloudflare establishes a second connection to the customer’s origin server to fetch the requested content, so it can respond to the original request. Protecting sensitive visitor data requires both of these connections to be secure against quantum attacks. We enabled post-quantum encryption support for both the visitor-to-Cloudflare (Connection 1) and Cloudflare-to-origin (Connection 2) connections in 2022 and 2023 , respectively, and already see significant usage . We are actively working on completing the picture with post-quantum authentication. For the visitor-to-Cloudflare connection, we are collaborating with Google and others at the Internet Engineering Task Force ( IETF ) to develop and experiment with Merkle Tree Certificates (MTC) , a design for fast, post-quantum certificates for the web, with initial deployments targeting 2027. The topic of this post, however, is the Cloudflare-to-origin connection, where the requirements for authentication differ from that of the visitor-to-Cloudflare connection in several important ways. For this connection, Cloudflare is the client. This gives us the control to employ techniques such as connection pooling to fan in requests from all over our network to a smaller set of connections to origin servers, amortizing the overhead of connection setup over many requests. This makes the cost of “drop-in” post-quantum signatures more palatable, and the performance benefits of MTC less necessary. And with a pre-existing trust relationship between Cloudflare and customers (i.e., a Cloudflare account), we need not tie ourselves to the constraints and timelines of the public key infrastructure (PKI) for the public Internet ( WebPKI ) and can instead use custom PKIs tailored to the use case, without overhead from intermediate certificates and Certificate Transparency that may not be applicable. Solutions like Cloudflare Tunnel can also be used to protect the Cloudflare-to-origin connection without upgrading legacy origin systems, by forwarding traffic over a tunnel secured with post-quantum encryption (and post-quantum authentication in the works). All this to say, the unique requirements of the Cloudflare-to-origin connection have allowed us to deploy post-quantum authentication via ML-DSA authentication ahead of support landing in the WebPKI for the public Internet. (For customers who stick with the WebPKI, don’t worry: we’ll add MTC support on the Cloudflare-to-origin connection in the future.) So how do you turn this on? Let’s dive into the configuration. Configuring fully PQ-secure origin connections We have added ML-DSA support (for all FIPS 204 parameter sets: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87) to the Custom Origin Trust Store and Authenticated Origin Pulls products. ML-DSA-44 is our recommendation for most applications as it is the most performant option and attains a comfortable NIST category 2 security strength. Custom Origin Trust Store When Cloudflare makes a connection to a customer origin server configured with Full (strict) SSL mode, we authenticate the origin certificate against a default trust store consisting of all commonly trusted Certificate Authorities (CAs) as well as Cloudflare’s origin CA . The Custom Origin Trust Store (COTS) product (which requires Advanced Certificate Manager to be enabled) allows customers to replace this default trust store with a set of CAs they control. COTS now allows customers to upload ML-DSA CAs, such that Cloudflare will trust any origin server certificate chaining to that CA when connecting to the origin. Authenticated Origin Pulls To limit abuse and resource consumption on their origin servers, customers may want to only serve requests coming from Cloudflare’s servers. Authenticated Origin Pulls (AOP) can be used to configure Cloudflare to present a client certificate to the origin server in order to establish a mutual TLS (mTLS) connection, in which communication between the parties is bidirectionally secure and trusted. AOP is available for free on all Cloudflare plan levels. AOP supports three configuration levels : global, per-zone, and per-hostname. The per-zone and per-hostname configuration levels now allow customers to upload ML-DSA certificates and private keys (in the FIPS 204 seed format), so that Cloudflare’s TLS client will present this certificate to authenticate itself when connecting to the origin server. (Don’t worry, we haven’t forgotten about the global configuration level — it just happens to be a more involved change that will be prioritized at a later date.) Avoiding downgrades Adding post-quantum encryption and authentication support to both the authenticating and verifying parties is necessary but not sufficient for full post-quantum security. The pesky issue of downgrades remains. If the verifying party supports any quantum-vulnerable authentication mechanisms, they remain open to attack from an on-path attacker capable of forging classical credentials. The fix: the verifying party must remove trust in quantum-vulnerable authentication mechanisms. (This is more nuanced in complex PKIs. For example, see the Chromium Security team’s four-stage plan for transitioning the Web.) See the configuration guide for AOP and COTS for details on how to ensure your origin is secure against downgrade attacks. Quick start The walkthrough below shows how to generate an ML-DSA certificate chain and configure both products via the Cloudflare API. For dashboard instructions and additional context, refer to the developer docs . 1. Generate certificates You will need OpenSSL 3.5.0 or later. The private key must be generated in the FIPS 204 seed-only encoding, which is the only format Cloudflare currently accepts on upload. Origin server certificate chain for COTS: Cloudflare client certificate chain for AOP: 2. Upload the origin CA to Custom Origin Trust Store Uploading a COTS CA replaces the default publicly-trusted CAs for the zone. Make sure you only upload post-quantum CAs if you want to avoid downgrade attacks. 3. Upload the client certificate for Authenticated Origin Pulls The example below uses zone-level AOP. If you prefer per-hostname AOP, use the /origin_tls_client_auth/hostnames/certificates endpoint instead. 4. Set your SSL/TLS mode to Full (strict) Custom Origin Trust Store is only active when your zone is using Full (strict) mode. If you are using AOP without COTS, Full or higher is sufficient. 5. Configure your origin server (on NGINX) If you are using COTS (your origin presents the ML-DSA server certificate): If you are using AOP (your origin verifies Cloudflare's client certificate): If you are using both together (recommended for full post-quantum mutual TLS): 6. Verify the post-quantum handshake The TLS handshake between Cloudflare and your origin happens behind the scenes, so you cannot observe it directly by connecting to your proxied hostname from the outside. Instead, verify each side separately. Verify COTS (origin presents an ML-DSA certificate): If your origin IP is directly reachable (for example, during testing before enabling the Cloudflare proxy), connect to the origin IP directly and validate the certificate: Look for Signature type: mldsa44 in the output. If your origin is firewalled to only accept Cloudflare IPs, check your origin server's TLS logs or use a packet capture tool such as ssldump or tcpdump on the origin to confirm that Cloudflare negotiated TLS 1.3 with the ML-DSA certificate. Verify AOP (Cloudflare presents a client certificate): Confirm that direct connections to the origin (without a valid client certificate) are rejected: With ssl_verify_client on enforced, this should fail with an SSL alert. Verify the full Cloudflare-to-origin path: Because the mTLS handshake happens server-to-server, the most reliable way to confirm that Cloudflare is presenting the ML-DSA client certificate is to inspect your origin server logs. For example, in NGINX you can log the client certificate serial number or subject: After sending a request through Cloudflare, check the log. You should see the serial number of the aop-client.crt certificate you uploaded. For the key agreement, ensure that your origin's TLS library supports X25519MLKEM768 and that it is preferred in your configuration. The post-quantum key agreement will be visible in origin server logs or packet captures as the negotiated group. The boring details Implementing this feature involved two primary systems: our control plane service that allows customers to manage their TLS settings and upload certificates, and the data plane service responsible for establishing TLS connections to origin servers based on customer configurations. Control plane As with many other services that power Cloudflare’s APIs and Dashboard, the service that powers the configuration for Cloudflare’s SSL/TLS products runs in a highly available setup across a set of critical data centers. The service is responsible for handling SSL/TLS settings updates and pushing them out to our globally-distributed key-value store so that they are available to data plane services when handling live requests. Enabling ML-DSA support for AOP and COTS required updating this service to support parsing and validating ML-DSA certificates. This sounds simple on paper, but there’s a catch: the service is written in Go, but Go’s standard X.509 and TLS libraries did not yet support ML-DSA. We instead implemented the necessary functionality in Cloudflare’s CIRCL library to patch in support. This was a relatively simple change, but repeating this for every service that needs post-quantum authentication support would be a major chore. Fortunately, Go 1.27 (expected August 2026) will include native ML-DSA support, and will allow us to drop the CIRCL dependency. Other Go-based services will then be able to seamlessly pull in ML-DSA support with a simple version update. Data plane With the control plane changes in place, customers could then upload ML-DSA certificates for the AOP and COTS products. The next step was to update our data plane service responsible for interacting with customer origins to actually use those certificates. We have talked in previous blog posts about our open-source proxy framework Pingora and specifically how we have a Pingora-based service that handles all the connections to those origins. That service is unimaginatively named Pingora Origin , and it is responsible for ensuring millions of requests per second worth of origin-bound requests make it safely and securely to their final destination. The task of ensuring the request’s security typically falls to the TLS provider, and it may surprise you to know that post-quantum security (or in this case authenticity) is no different. It also might come as a letdown that defending against quantum attacks does not require exotic states of matter with lasers and superconducting Josephson junctions ; all you need is an update to BoringSSL . Now, BoringSSL lives up to its name: over the past several years, there have been no CVEs or major changes. In fact, we relied on that stability so heavily that we have an admission to make: we snoozed Pingora Origin’s update to BoringSSL for four years, instead maintaining an internal fork to patch in additional functionality as needed. That has worked well, but when post-quantum authentication support landed in BoringSSL in April 2026, we decided that this update was worth the inconvenience. This is where we wish we could say, “This update went perfectly. No notes!” but naturally there were some hiccups. Within the four years’ worth of code changes was this commit that enables enforcement of rules related to KeyUsage in TLS certificates. This change is in line with the specifications, but as we have seen before, the Internet is not known for being RFC compliant . The result was that even after testing the changes for weeks and a very slow release rollout looking for just this sort of regression, a small number of customers’ certificates were deemed invalid after the change, leading to an incident on June 10, 2026 . We quickly rolled back the change and after a patch to retain support for RSA certificates with technically invalid KeyUsage , fully post-quantum secure TLS to origins is now live and ready to use. We are only getting started ML-DSA support is increasingly ubiquitous across TLS libraries , and routine software updates will bring post-quantum authentication support to many applications. (Please keep your libraries updated!) The highly-anticipated Go 1.27 (August 2026) will come with native ML-DSA support, allowing Go-based services to add post-quantum authentication with a simple version update. As these changes propagate across the ecosystem, we will be upgrading our systems as well. See PQC in Cloudflare Products for an up-to-date tracker of post-quantum encryption and authentication support in Cloudflare products and services.
